title: Throughput + Latency Quickframe for Integration Architects (Draft)
content:
Purpose:
Short, usable reference for sellers talking to Integration Architects and Platform Engineers about throughput vs latency tradeoffs, recommended Redwood configurations, and canned responses to common objections. Meant as a one-page flip + 6 speaker bullets. Draft — please add missing numbers and local region examples.

Target persona:
- Integration Architect at an engineering-led company (SMB -> midmarket).
- Care about predictable tail latency, cost per request, and predictable concurrency.
- Often owns API gateway, rate limits, and capacity planning.

Quick elevator (30s):
- "Redwood lets you serve LLMs with predictable latency at scale by giving you observable SLOs, configurable batching, and fallbacks to tuned model variants. For engineering teams you get a clear throughput/lambda cost model and simple knobs to trade cost for lower P50/P95 latencies."

Key selling levers to call out (talk track bullet points):
1) Dedicated capacity: commit to reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and remove noisy neighbor risk — good for high-concurrency endpoints.
2) Smart routing & fallbacks: route by latency budget -> fallback to cheaper quantized model when under pressure. Keeps application response time SLA without over-provisioning.
3) Batching + prefix cache: automatically reduces token cost for high-QPS short prompts; show typical 1.5-3x effective throughput improvement on repetitive prompts.
4) Observability: token-level cost/latency breakdown, per-route histograms, and KV cache hit-rate dashboards for tuning.
5) Canary + A/B rollouts: canary model variants to validate latency regressions before global rollouts.

Common objections + short responses (1-2 lines each):
- “We can host models ourselves, cheaper.”
  "Self-hosting shifts MTTI/MTTR and ops cost to your team. Redwood buys you predictable latency SLOs and operational primitives (routing, canary, cache) you otherwise build and maintain — often more expensive than the delta in GPU costs."

- “Batching increases latency for single-user requests.”
  "We provide latency budget-aware batching: low-latency routes can opt out or use micro-batches; analytical routes can take advantage of larger batches for cost efficiency."

- "Quantized models hurt quality."
  "Recommend canary with a small prompt set and quality gates. For most retrieval-augmented flows quality delta is minimal while cost drops 2-4x."

- "What about peak traffic and bursty events?"
  "Dedicated pools + configured burst capacity handle planned spikes; for emergency fallback we route to a compatible lower-cost region or model to keep tails short."

Numbers cheat (placeholder values — replace with customer-specific numbers before calls):
- Typical P50: 60–120 ms (short prompts, hosted), P95: 200–450 ms depending on model size and KV cache hit rate.
- Throughput: 100–800 RPS per GPU (varies widely by model, sequence length, batching).
- Cost: quantized variant often 30–60% lower per-token.
- Batching wins: 1.5–3.0x throughput improvement on repeated/templated prompts.

Guided Config recommendations (quickmap):
- Low latency (<150 ms P95): dedicated capacity, micro-batching (or batching disabled), KV cache enabled, single-region routing.
- Balanced (cost + latency): shared hosted with autoscale, conservative batching, quantized model for tails.
- Cost-first: larger batch windows, quantized models, async/queue approach for non-interactive flows.

Slide outline for a 6-slide quick deck (speaker notes in parens):
1) Title + 1-line thesis (why throughput/latency matters to platform teams).
2) What Integration Architects care about (latency SLOs, predictability, cost).
3) How Redwood maps to those concerns (dedicated, routing, batching, observability).
4) Example configurations (low-latency vs cost-first).
5) Live checklist for canary & fallback (what to verify before rollout).
6) Ask + next steps (POC parameters, sample SLAs, contact).

Canary & rollout checklist (quick):
- Baseline metrics captured (P50/P95/P99) before canary.
- 5–10% traffic canary for 24–72 hours (longer for stateful flows).
- Compare token cost and KV cache hit-rate.
- Automated rollback on error rate or latency regression thresholds.

Customer-specific prep questions (ask when booking technical discovery):
- Typical prompt length (tokens) and variance?
- What latency budget do you commit to for user-facing flows (P95)?
- Peak QPS and expected concurrency per endpoint?
- Any regulatory region constraints (data residency)?
- Do you have a preferred fallback model/quality threshold?

Open / TODO (notes to self):
- Pull region-specific latency numbers from infra team (APAC EU US).
- Add short comparative table of GPU types (A10G vs H100) and throughput estimates.
- Build a canned notebook for on-call demo showing cache/route swap and effect on P95.
- Validate P50/P95 placeholders with bench results from serving-runtime team.

Format notes for seller:
- Keep the first slide super terse — integration architects love short, actionable specs.
- Use real numbers where possible; replace the placeholders.
- Bring an infra diagram for the first customer call (routing + fallback path).

Quick call checklist for seller (before demo):
- Confirm sample prompts and tokens, send test creds for demo environment.
- Prepare 2 configurations (low-latency vs cost-optimized) to flip live.
- Prepare a canary plan: traffic % and rollback thresholds.

End of draft.
Comments welcome — tag @AvaMartinez in Slack thread #g2m-enablement for updates.
